segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Take care not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that people will praise them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you pray, you are not to be like the performers; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the main streets, so that people will see them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you pray, do not babble on like the Gentiles, for they think they will be heard because of their many words.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You, then, are to pray like this: ‘Our Father in the heavens, may your name be held holy,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: may your kingdom come, may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Give us today our daily bread,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the performers, for they make their faces unsightly so that people will see them fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that your fasting will be seen not by people but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if your eye is stingy, your whole body will be full of darkness. So if the light within you is darkness, how great that darkness is!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one can be a slave to two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot be a slave to both God and wealth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they are?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And which of you by worrying can add a single hour to your span of life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And why do you worry about clothing? Consider how the lilies of the field grow: they do not labor or spin.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you of little faith?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry, saying, ‘What are we to eat?’ or ‘What are we to drink?’ or ‘What are we to wear?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For it is the Gentiles who seek after all these things; and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

notes.note: Here the word means doing what is right in practice. It heads the three examples that follow: giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so the same word can elsewhere be rendered 'justice'.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 9, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses often for God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it and the singular where the Greek is singular, as in verses 10 and 20.

The Greek word originally meant a stage actor, but in Jewish Greek before the New Testament it already meant a godless or insincere person, and elsewhere this translation renders it 'hypocrites'. In this chapter the passage is about religion staged for an audience, with trumpets, street corners and being seen. The theatrical sense is therefore live, and 'performers' is used in verses 2, 5 and 16.

notes.phrase: they have been paid their reward in full
notes.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts from the period for acknowledging payment in full, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone. The account is settled and nothing further is owed. Many modern translations similarly render 'they have received their reward in full'.

The Greek verb is extremely rare and its exact sense is uncertain. Its meaning is inferred mainly from the parallel 'many words' later in the verse. Proposals include babbling, stammering and repeating empty phrases.

notes.phrase: may your name be held holy
notes.note: 'Hallowed' is the traditional word but is now archaic. The Greek is a request that God's name be treated as holy, matching the two requests that follow. It may ask that people honor the name, that God act to vindicate it, or both. The Greek passive leaves that open.

This Greek word is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer, and its meaning is uncertain. The main proposals are 'for the coming day', 'necessary for existence' and 'for today'. With no secure alternative, the traditional 'daily' is kept.

The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person and an enticement to sin, whereas English 'temptation' now suggests only the second. Many scholars take the petition as asking to be spared a time of trial, and some think specifically of the final ordeal before the end. The traditional sense remains possible.

The Greek form can be masculine ('the evil one', meaning the devil) or neuter ('evil' in general), and the grammar does not settle it. Matthew clearly uses the expression for the devil elsewhere, which favors the personal reading, but both are widely held.

notes.phrase: rescue us from the evil one
notes.traditional: For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.
notes.note: The familiar closing doxology is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not part of the SBLGNT text translated here. It appears in later manuscripts in varying forms. It is generally thought to have entered the text from the prayer's early use in worship.

The Greek word means 'single' or 'sound', and most translations keep the physical image with 'healthy'. The saying sits between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth, however, and the contrasting 'evil eye' was a Jewish idiom for stinginess. The saying is therefore taken to be about generosity. The physical picture of a sound eye is lost in this rendering.

Literally 'if your eye is evil'. In Jewish usage an 'evil eye' meant a grudging, miserly attitude toward others, as in Matthew 20:15, not the casting of a curse. Translations that keep the physical image render 'bad' or 'unhealthy'.

The verb is the ordinary word for a slave's service to an owner, and 'masters' here are slave-owners. The point is that a slave belongs wholly to one master. 'Serve' in modern English suggests employment, which can be shared between employers.

The Greek text keeps an Aramaic word, mamona, meaning wealth or property, which older English versions carried over as 'mammon'. In sources of the period it is an ordinary word and not the name of a god or demon. The personification comes from setting it beside God as a rival master.

notes.phrase: a single hour to your span of life
notes.traditional: add one cubit unto his stature
notes.note: The Greek says literally 'add one cubit', a measure of length of about half a metre. The noun that follows can mean either age or bodily height. Most modern translations take it as a measure of length applied figuratively to lifespan, since adding a cubit to one's height would be no small thing. The older rendering takes it of stature.

Many manuscripts read 'the kingdom of God and his righteousness'. The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading, literally 'the kingdom and his righteousness', where 'his' refers to the heavenly Father of verse 32. The pronoun is taken here with both nouns.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, James, 1 Peter and Revelation, where 'temptation', 'trial' and 'testing' compete and the choice changes what the reader thinks is being asked or described.
The δοῦλος word-family is frequent in the Gospels and Paul, and wavering between 'serve' and 'be a slave to' would obscure the slavery image.
An Aramaic word kept in the Greek here and in Luke 16; translators divide between 'mammon', 'money' and 'wealth', and it should be handled the same way in both books.
Jesus' formula 'Amen I tell you' occurs dozens of times across all four Gospels and needs one rendering (truly / amen / I assure you) throughout.
Recurs in the Gospels and Paul where 'trespasses', 'sins', 'transgressions' and 'offenses' are all in use, and it needs to stay distinct from ἁμαρτία.
